title: How can several local tests prove irreducibility?
summary: Different local tests constrain the same hypothetical factor degree. Their intersection can be empty even when every modular reduction is reducible.
scope: Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[X]\) be monic and separable, of degree \(n\ge2\), with \(f(0)\ne0\).

edges.label: Reduction of factors
edges.explanation: Gauss’s lemma and monicity preserve the degree of every rational factor after reduction; its degree is a subset sum, counting modular factors with multiplicity.

edges.label: Root valuations
edges.explanation: On an edge of reduced slope −a/b, each local factor uses a multiple of b roots, bounded by the edge length.

edges.label: Necessary restrictions
edges.explanation: Intersect the degree sets supplied by the selected modular factorizations.

edges.label: Necessary restrictions
edges.explanation: Include the degree sets supplied by every selected Newton polygon in the same intersection.

edges.label: If the intersection is empty
edges.explanation: A proper rational factor would have a positive degree below n belonging to every displayed degree set, contradicting an empty intersection.

edges.label: Factor–orbit correspondence
edges.explanation: For a separable polynomial, irreducible factors correspond to Galois orbits on the roots; one factor is equivalent to one orbit.

sources.note: The subset-sum restriction is the direct reduction-of-factors consequence used here.
The root–slope theorem; integrality of a slope factor’s constant-term valuation gives the denominator restriction.
Explicit Newton degree sets and their intersection; the present map also includes modular degree sets.

body:
If the irreducible modular factor degrees at a prime \(p\), repeated according to multiplicity, are \(d_{p,1},\ldots,d_{p,r}\), every proper rational factor has degree in

\[D_p=\left\{\sum_{i\in I}d_{p,i}:I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\right\}\cap\{1,\ldots,n-1\}.\]

If the Newton edges at a prime \(q\) have reduced slopes \(-a_j/b_j\), with \(b_j>0\), and horizontal lengths \(L_j\), the corresponding restriction is

\[N_q=\left\{\sum_j b_jk_j: k_j\in\mathbb Z,\ 0\le k_j\le L_j/b_j\right\}\cap\{1,\ldots,n-1\}.\]

Thus \(\bigcap_pD_p\cap\bigcap_qN_q=\varnothing\) proves irreducibility. One may use either kind of test alone. These are necessary degree restrictions; they do not assert that each permitted degree actually occurs. Squarefree reduction is unnecessary for this argument, but modular multiplicities must be counted.

The quartic example above has \(D_2=\{1,3\}\) and \(D_3=\{2\}\). Two reducible reductions therefore certify rational irreducibility. The degree-six exponential example gives the parallel Newton-polygon certificate \(N_2=\{2,4\}\), \(N_3=\{3\}\).

related.label: Use squarefree reductions to obtain cycle types

title: How do two modular factorizations determine S₅?
summary: One prime proves transitivity; another supplies a transposition. Prime degree supplies primitivity, and the two branches together determine the full group.
scope: Let \(f=X^5-X-1\) and \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)\), acting on its five roots.

edges.label: Reduction criterion
edges.explanation: The monic degree-five polynomial retains its degree modulo 3, so irreducible reduction proves irreducibility over the rationals.

edges.label: One irreducible factor
edges.explanation: Irreducibility is equivalent to transitivity of the Galois action on the five roots.

edges.label: Prime degree 5
edges.explanation: In a transitive action block sizes divide the degree; prime degree has no nontrivial block sizes.

edges.label: Dedekind–Frobenius
edges.explanation: The reduction modulo 2 is squarefree, and its irreducible factors have degrees 2 and 3; the Galois group therefore contains that cycle type.

edges.label: Cube the permutation
edges.explanation: The two cycles are disjoint; cubing kills the 3-cycle and leaves the 2-cycle.

edges.label: Primitivity
edges.explanation: Primitivity is one of the two hypotheses required by the transposition criterion.

edges.label: A transposition
edges.explanation: The existence of a transposition is the second hypothesis required by the criterion.

edges.label: Primitive + transposition
edges.explanation: A primitive permutation group containing a transposition is the full symmetric group.

sources.note: The factor–orbit theorem and the modular computation for this quintic; taking the cube is also checked directly.
Lemma 10 gives prime-degree primitivity; Lemma 6 gives the primitive-group transposition criterion.

body:
The complete arithmetic certificate is

\[\begin{aligned}f\bmod2&=(X^2+X+1)(X^3+X^2+1),\\ f\bmod3&\text{ is irreducible},\\ \operatorname{disc}(f)&=2869=19\cdot151.\end{aligned}\]

The two factors modulo \(2\) are irreducible: each has degree two or three and neither has a root in \(\mathbb F_2\). Their distinctness makes the reduction squarefree. For an exact check modulo \(3\), polynomial arithmetic gives \(X^{3^5}\equiv X\pmod f\) and \(\gcd(f,X^3-X)=1\). The finite-field irreducibility criterion for prime degree five then applies. The discriminant calculation independently confirms that both primes are good.

The left branch excludes nontrivial block systems. The right produces a permutation exchanging exactly two roots: if \(\sigma=(ab)(cde)\), then \(\sigma^3=(ab)\). Both properties are needed for the final group criterion. Transitivity and a transposition alone do not suffice in composite degree; the order-eight dihedral action on four points is a counterexample.

The same group certificate has a geometric consequence: Zarhin’s theorem applies to \(y^2=X^5-X-1\), whose genus-two Jacobian has geometric endomorphism ring \(\mathbb Z\).

related.label: Why primitivity and a transposition imply Sₙ
From S₅ to a Jacobian with endomorphism ring ℤ

title: When does a reciprocal polynomial have the full signed group?
summary: Passing to inverse pairs halves the degree. Recovering the full group then requires both the permutation group on pairs and independent quadratic extensions.
scope: Let \(K\) have characteristic different from \(2\), and let \(q\in K[Y]\) be monic and separable of degree \(m\ge1\), with \(q(2)q(-2)\ne0\). Put \(f(X)=X^m q(X+X^{-1})\).

edges.label: Collapse inverse pairs
edges.explanation: The map α↦α+α⁻¹ identifies inverse pairs with roots of q, and restriction surjects onto the Galois group of q.

edges.label: Solve X² − yᵢX + 1
edges.explanation: Writing M for the splitting field of q, the quadratic formula gives the splitting field L=M(√(y₁²−4),…,√(yₘ²−4)).

edges.label: Kummer theory
edges.explanation: If r is the dimension of the span of the radicand square classes in M×/M×², then [L:M]=2ʳ.

edges.label: Test the quotient
edges.explanation: The condition to verify is that the quotient on the m inverse pairs is the full symmetric group; it is not automatic.

edges.label: Test r = m
edges.explanation: The condition to verify is maximal square-class rank m; it is not automatic from irreducibility.

edges.label: Full quotient
edges.explanation: The full quotient is the first necessary and sufficient condition in the joint criterion.

edges.label: Full kernel
edges.explanation: Independent square classes give the full order-2ᵐ kernel, the second condition in the joint criterion.

edges.label: Full quotient and full kernel
edges.explanation: The Galois group embeds in C₂≀Sₘ; it equals that group exactly when its quotient has order m! and its kernel has order 2ᵐ.

sources.note: Trace substitution, quadratic lifting, signed-permutation action, and the discriminant identity. The same algebraic formulas hold over any field of characteristic different from 2.
Kummer correspondence, extension degree, and perfect pairing, applied with exponent 2 over the splitting field M.

body:
Let \(y_1,\ldots,y_m\) be the roots of \(q\), let \(M\) be its splitting field, and put \(d_i=y_i^2-4\). The assumptions imply \(d_i\ne0\) and make \(f\) separable. Its splitting field is

\[L=M(\sqrt{d_1},\ldots,\sqrt{d_m}),\qquad [L:M]=2^{\dim_{\mathbb F_2}\langle[d_1],\ldots,[d_m]\rangle}.\]

The square classes are taken in \(M^\times/M^{\times2}\), not in the base field. Restriction gives an exact sequence

\[1\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(L/M)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(f/K)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(q/K)\longrightarrow1.\]

Consequently, \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/K)=C_2\wr S_m\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Gal}(q/K)=S_m\) and all \(m\) radicand classes are independent. This follows by comparing orders inside the natural signed-permutation group; no splitting of the displayed exact sequence is assumed in advance.

For example, \(q=Y^2-3\) has group \(S_2\), but its lift is \(f=X^4-X^2+1=\Phi_{12}\). Both radicands are \(-1\), so the kernel has rank one and \(\operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)=C_2\times C_2\), of order four rather than eight.

The identity \(\operatorname{disc}(f)=q(2)q(-2)\operatorname{disc}(q)^2\) detects parity, not the full kernel. A square discriminant forces even total pair flips. For even polynomials \(q(X^2)\), assuming also \(q(0)\ne0\), the same method uses opposite pairs and radicands \(y_i\); this connects directly to parity-reduced Legendre and Hermite polynomials.
